theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you take apart a bench grinder that plugs into a socket, what is the first thing to do?
options: Switch it off at its own switch only
Remove its guards and tool rest
Unplug it and keep the plug where you can see it
Spray it with water to cool it down

questions.stem: A pump motor is wired to a fixed isolator. Before you take the motor apart, what must be done?
options: Isolate, lock off, tag and prove it dead
Switch it off at the start button only
Remove the fuse and leave it on the board
Ask the operator not to switch it on

questions.stem: Why must the capacitor of a capacitor-start motor be discharged before you handle it?
options: It may leak oil onto the windings
It will make the motor run backwards
It can make the bearings seize
It can hold a charge that gives a shock

questions.stem: How should a motor capacitor be discharged?
options: By shorting its terminals with a screwdriver
With a resistor discharge tool
By leaving it in the sun for an hour
By tapping it with a hammer

questions.stem: Where would you find the correct order for taking apart a motor you have not seen before?
options: The maker's service manual or exploded diagram
On the motor's terminal box cover
On the plug of the power cord
In the electrical code book

questions.stem: Why should you take photos and make notes before you disconnect a motor's wiring?
options: To show the customer how dirty it was
To sell the photos to the maker
So it can be reconnected correctly
So you do not need to test it later

questions.stem: Before you remove the end shields (end bells) of a motor, why do you make match marks on them and the frame?
options: To show where the bolts were tightest
To show which end is heavier
To check the frame is earthed
So they go back in the same position

questions.stem: How should you keep the small parts as you take a motor apart?
options: In your pocket so they do not get lost
In labelled trays in the order removed
On the floor under the bench
Mixed in one box with other jobs

questions.stem: Which tool is used to remove a tight pulley from a motor shaft?
options: A cold chisel and club hammer
A pipe wrench on the pulley rim
A gear (pulley) puller
Long-nose pliers

questions.stem: How should a tight end shield be loosened from the motor frame?
options: Tap it evenly with a soft-faced mallet
Prise it off with a large screwdriver
Hit it hard with a steel hammer
Heat it with a gas torch

questions.stem: When you pull the rotor out of the stator, what must you avoid?
options: Holding it by the shaft
Dragging it against the stator windings
Supporting its weight with both hands
Keeping it straight as it comes out

questions.stem: When pulling a ball bearing off a shaft, where should the puller press?
options: On the outer race
On the bearing shield or seal
On the end of the winding
On the inner race

questions.stem: How can you tell that a ball bearing is worn?
options: It feels rough, noisy or loose when turned
It is shiny and turns smoothly
It has a little grease on it
Its number is printed on the side

questions.stem: In a universal motor, such as the one in an electric drill, what do the carbon brushes rub against?
options: The stator windings
The bearings
The commutator
The cooling fan

questions.stem: When should carbon brushes be replaced?
options: Every time the motor is switched on
When they turn black in colour
Only when the motor will not start
When worn to the length the maker gives

questions.stem: What does heavy sparking at the commutator of a running motor usually show?
options: The motor is working normally
Worn brushes or a dirty or worn commutator
The motor needs a bigger fuse
The bearings have far too much grease packed in them

questions.stem: In a split-phase motor, what does the centrifugal switch do?
options: Reverses the motor when it gets hot
Keeps the motor running at full speed
Cuts out the start winding at speed
Stops the motor if the load is too high

questions.stem: Which test checks that a motor winding is not shorted to the frame?
options: Insulation resistance test
Continuity test of the winding
Speed test with a tachometer
Current test with a clamp meter

questions.stem: A continuity test across a motor winding shows an infinite (open) reading. What does this mean?
options: The winding is in good order
The winding is broken
The bearings are worn
The capacitor is charged

questions.stem: You take a motor apart and the windings are dark and smell burnt. What does this suggest?
options: The motor is new
The bearings need grease
The motor has been run too slowly
The windings have overheated

questions.stem: Which is a safe way to clean dust out of a motor's windings?
options: A soft brush and dry, low-pressure air
Wash the windings with a hose
Soak the stator in petrol overnight
Scrape the windings with a knife

questions.stem: If a solvent is used to clean metal parts, what must you do?
options: Use it next to a gas flame so the parts dry fast
Use petrol because it is cheap
Use it in a ventilated area, with gloves
Keep the windings soaking in it

questions.stem: A bearing must be replaced. Which new bearing should you fit?
options: Any bearing that slides onto the shaft
One with the same size and type number
The cheapest bearing in the store
A bigger bearing so it lasts longer

questions.stem: How should a new ball bearing be fitted onto a motor shaft?
options: Hit the outer race hard with a steel hammer
Heat it red-hot with a gas torch
Press on the seal until it moves
Press it on by the inner race with a tube

questions.stem: A motor has sealed ball bearings. How are they lubricated?
options: Fill them with oil every week
Pack extra grease in through the seal
They are greased for life by the maker
Spray them with water to cool them

questions.stem: In what order are parts usually put back when you reassemble a motor?
options: The reverse of the order they came out
Any order, as long as all the parts go in
The heaviest parts first, the rest later
The order in which they were cleaned

questions.stem: How should the end shield bolts be tightened during reassembly?
options: One bolt fully tight, then the next
As tight as possible with a long bar
Only finger tight so they can move
A little at a time, in a criss-cross order

questions.stem: After reassembly, what is the first check that the motor is put together correctly?
options: Plug it in and run it at once
Turn the shaft by hand to check it is free
Weigh it to see that no parts are missing
Shake it to listen for loose parts

questions.stem: Why do you test the continuity between the motor frame and the earth pin of its plug?
options: To show the frame is earthed in case of a fault
To check how fast the motor will run
To check the plug fuse is the right size
To find out the resistance of the run winding

questions.stem: Who should carry out the first run test of a reassembled motor at the Centre?
options: Any trainee, as soon as it is together
The customer, at home
The instructor, on a protected test bench
Nobody; motors are never run after repair

questions.stem: What are the main parts of a contactor?
options: Rotor, stator and brushes
Coil, armature, contacts and springs
Bearings, shaft and fan
Capacitor, centrifugal switch and winding

questions.stem: The contacts of a contactor are badly burnt and pitted. What is usually done?
options: Fill the pits with solder
Paint them with silver paint
File them down until they are thin and smooth again
Replace them with the maker's contact kit

questions.stem: How do you check the coil of a relay when the relay is isolated?
options: Measure its insulation to the contacts only
Look to see if the case is clean
Measure its resistance with an ohmmeter
Press the armature in with a screwdriver

questions.stem: When you take apart a contactor or relay, why must you take care with the springs?
options: They are under tension and can fly out
They carry the main current to the load terminals
They are made of glass
They hold the coil voltage

questions.stem: What does a solenoid do when its coil is energised?
options: It makes heat to warm a liquid
It pulls a plunger in by magnetism
It stores charge like a capacitor
It measures the current in a circuit

questions.stem: What does an exploded diagram show?
options: The wiring inside the panel
How a part will break apart when a fault occurs
The speed of the motor
How the parts fit together, spread apart

questions.stem: Which tool removes a circlip from a motor shaft?
options: Circlip pliers
Side cutting pliers
A pipe wrench
A cold chisel

questions.stem: A pulley is held on by a grub screw with a hexagon socket. Which tool is used?
options: A flat-blade screwdriver
A pipe wrench
A hex key of the right size
Combination pliers with a firm grip

questions.stem: Why use a torque wrench on bolts and terminals when you reassemble?
options: To make the work go faster
So bolts can be tightened past the limit
So the bolts can be removed by hand later
To tighten to the value the maker gives

questions.stem: A motor weighs about 30 kg. How should it be moved to the bench?
options: One person carries it on their shoulder
Two people or a lifting aid
Roll it along the floor by its shaft
Lift it by its terminal box

questions.stem: An insulation resistance test between a winding and the frame gives a very low reading. What should you do?
options: Run the motor to dry it out
Pass it because it is a small motor
Find the fault before it is used
Connect the frame to neutral instead

questions.stem: After a motor is reconnected, it turns the wrong way. What is the most likely cause?
options: The winding leads were reconnected wrongly
The bearings were fitted on the wrong way round
The brushes are too new
The fan is dirty

questions.stem: What should be written on the job card after repairing a motor?
options: The colour of the motor paint
The time you had lunch
The names of other trainees in the room
The parts replaced and the test results

questions.stem: What should be done with old bearings, worn brushes and used cleaning rags?
options: Leave them inside the motor
Put them in the right waste bins
Throw them in the drain
Keep them in the parts tray for next time

questions.stem: Before a reassembled fan is handed back, what must be checked?
options: That the blades are painted
That the plug has been changed to a new colour
That all guards and covers are refitted
That the motor is warm

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: A capacitor-start motor on a water pump is fixed in place and wired to an isolator. Describe how you would make it safe before you take it apart.
essays.modelAnswer: I would tell the person in charge that the pump will be off, and find the correct isolator. I would switch off the isolator, fit a lock so that nobody can switch it back on, and fix a tag with my name, the date and the reason, keeping the key. Then I would check my voltage tester on a proving unit or a known live source, and test at the motor terminals between every pair of conductors and each conductor to earth, to prove the motor is dead. I would check the tester again on the known source to make sure it did not fail. Next I would deal with the capacitor, which can hold a charge even when the supply is off. I would discharge it with a resistor discharge tool as the maker's instructions say, then check it with a meter. Only then would I disconnect the wiring and start, following the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Informs the person in charge and finds the correct isolator
Switches off, locks off and tags, keeping the key
Checks the tester before use, proves dead at the motor terminals, checks the tester after
Discharges the capacitor safely with a resistor tool and checks it
Only then disconnects and starts work

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan and record your work so that a motor can be put back together correctly after it is taken apart.
essays.modelAnswer: Before I start, I would read the maker's service manual and look at the exploded diagram to see how the parts fit together and in what order they come off. I would collect the right tools, such as spanners, a soft-faced mallet, a puller and circlip pliers, and set out a clean bench with labelled trays. Before disconnecting anything, I would photograph the terminal box and write down which lead goes to which terminal, and fit labels to the leads. I would make match marks on the end shields and the frame with a centre punch or marker so they go back the same way. As I remove each part, I would put it in a tray in order and note anything special, such as spacer washers or which way a part faces. I would write down the nameplate details and any damage I find. These notes and photos let me reassemble the motor in the reverse order with nothing missed.
markingPoints: Reads the service manual and exploded diagram
Gathers the right tools and sets up a clean bench with labelled trays
Photographs and labels the wiring before disconnecting
Makes match marks on the end shields and frame
Keeps parts in order and notes details, so reassembly is the reverse order

essays.stem: Describe the steps to take apart a small single-phase induction motor once it has been made safe.
essays.modelAnswer: With the motor isolated, proved dead, the capacitor discharged and the wiring recorded and disconnected, I would move the motor to a clean bench. I would make match marks on the end shields and the frame. Next I would remove the pulley or coupling with a gear puller, after taking out any grub screw and the key, and remove the fan cover and fan. I would undo the end shield bolts, keeping them in a labelled tray. Then I would loosen the end shields by tapping them evenly with a soft-faced mallet, never a steel hammer. I would remove the end shield on the side away from the shaft extension, then carefully draw the rotor out, keeping it straight and holding its weight so it does not drag on the stator windings. I would put the rotor on a soft, clean surface. If the bearings must come off, I would use a bearing puller that presses on the inner race.
markingPoints: Starts only when isolated, proved dead, capacitor discharged and wiring recorded
Makes match marks and removes pulley, key, fan cover and fan with the right tools
Removes bolts into a tray and loosens end shields with a soft-faced mallet
Draws the rotor out straight without touching the windings
Removes bearings, if needed, with a puller on the inner race

essays.stem: Describe how to remove a worn ball bearing from a motor shaft and fit a new one correctly.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check that the bearing really is worn by turning it by hand: a worn bearing feels rough, sounds noisy or has play. I would note the number on the bearing so the new one is the same size and type. To remove it, I would set up a bearing puller so that its jaws press on the inner race, the part fitted to the shaft, and turn the screw slowly and evenly. I would not hammer the bearing or the end of the shaft. I would clean the shaft and check it for scoring or damage. To fit the new bearing, I would keep it clean and in its packet until needed. I would press it on by the inner race only, using a press or a clean tube that fits the inner race, pushing it square until it seats against the shoulder. I would never press on the outer race or the seal. Some workshops warm bearings with a bearing heater, as the maker says, but never with a flame.
markingPoints: Confirms wear and notes the bearing number for a like-for-like replacement
Removes it with a puller pressing on the inner race; no hammering
Cleans and checks the shaft
Fits the new bearing by pressing on the inner race only, square to the shoulder
Keeps the bearing clean; no flame heating; follows the maker's instructions

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect the parts of a dismantled single-phase motor for wear and damage.
essays.modelAnswer: I would clean the parts first so that I can see them clearly. I would turn each bearing by hand and replace any that feel rough, are noisy or have play. I would check the shaft for scoring, a bent shaft or a damaged keyway. I would look at the stator windings for dark or burnt insulation, a burnt smell, broken leads or loose ties. I would check the rotor for rub marks, which show that a bearing was worn or the rotor was touching the stator. In a split-phase or capacitor-start motor, I would check the centrifugal switch: its contacts should not be burnt and its weights and springs should move freely. I would check the capacitor for bulging or leaks. I would test the windings for continuity and test insulation resistance from the windings to the frame. I would also check the end shields for cracks, and the fan and terminal box for damage. All faults are written on the job card.
markingPoints: Cleans the parts first and checks bearings by hand
Checks shaft, keyway and rotor for damage or rub marks
Checks windings for burnt insulation, smell and loose leads
Checks the centrifugal switch and the capacitor
Tests continuity and insulation resistance, and records all faults

essays.stem: Explain how you would replace the carbon brushes in a portable electric drill and check the commutator.
essays.modelAnswer: I would unplug the drill and keep the plug where I can see it. I would read the maker's instructions to find how the brushes are reached; on many drills they are behind caps on the side, but on some the case must be opened. I would note how each brush sits and which way it faces, then remove the old brushes and measure them. If they are worn to the length the maker gives, or are chipped or uneven, I would replace both brushes with the maker's correct type. I would look at the commutator: it should be smooth and brown, without deep grooves, burnt bars or raised segments. Light dirt can be cleaned as the maker says; a badly worn commutator needs a specialist repair. I would fit the new brushes so they slide freely in their holders and the springs press them onto the commutator. Then I would reassemble the case and test the earth continuity or check it is double insulated, before an instructor does a run test.
markingPoints: Unplugs and keeps the plug in view; reads the maker's instructions
Notes the brush positions and measures them against the maker's length
Replaces both brushes with the correct type
Inspects the commutator for grooves, burnt bars or raised segments
Brushes slide freely with spring pressure; reassembles and tests before a supervised run test

essays.stem: Describe how you would take apart, inspect and reassemble a contactor that has been isolated.
essays.modelAnswer: With the control panel isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead, I would label and record all the wires on the contactor before removing it. On the bench I would read the maker's instructions, then remove the cover or arc chute and take out the moving contacts, the armature and the springs, keeping them in order in a tray. I would take care with the springs because they are under tension and can fly out, so I would wear safety glasses. I would inspect the contacts: if they are badly burnt or pitted, I would fit the maker's contact kit, not file them thin. I would check that the armature and the faces of the magnet are clean and not damaged, and that the springs are not broken. I would measure the coil resistance with an ohmmeter and compare it with the expected value. Then I would reassemble in the reverse order, check that the armature moves freely by hand, and refit and reconnect the contactor as recorded.
markingPoints: Panel isolated and proved dead; wiring labelled and recorded
Dismantles in order, taking care with springs and wearing eye protection
Inspects contacts and replaces with the maker's kit if badly worn
Checks the armature, magnet faces and springs; measures coil resistance
Reassembles in reverse order, checks free movement and reconnects as recorded

essays.stem: Describe how you would reassemble a single-phase motor and the checks you would make as you go.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make sure all the parts are clean and that any new parts, such as bearings, are the right type. I would work in the reverse order of dismantling, using my notes and photos. I would fit the bearings to the shaft by the inner race, then guide the rotor carefully into the stator, keeping it straight so it does not touch the windings. I would fit the end shields with their match marks lined up, and put in the bolts. I would tighten the bolts a little at a time in a criss-cross order, turning the shaft by hand as I go to check that it stays free and does not rub. Then I would check the end float. I would refit the fan, the fan cover, the key and the pulley. I would reconnect the leads in the terminal box as recorded and tighten them to the maker's torque. Finally I would make sure that no parts are left over in the tray.
markingPoints: Clean parts, correct replacements, reverse order using notes and photos
Fits the rotor carefully without touching the windings
Lines up match marks and tightens bolts evenly in a criss-cross order
Turns the shaft by hand to check it is free; checks end float
Refits fan, cover, key and pulley; reconnects as recorded; no parts left over

essays.stem: Describe the tests you would do on a reassembled motor before it goes back into service.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would turn the shaft by hand to check that it turns freely and quietly, with a little end float. Then, with the motor still disconnected from any supply, I would do the dead tests. I would test the continuity of each winding with an ohmmeter; a low reading shows the winding is not broken, and an open reading means a fault. I would do an insulation resistance test between the windings and the frame, using the test voltage the tester and the Centre's rules give, usually 500 V DC for a 110 V or 220 V motor. A high reading in megohms shows good insulation. I would test the continuity from the motor frame to the earth terminal or the earth pin of its plug. If all the dead tests pass, the motor can have a run test, done by the instructor or a competent person on a protected test bench, checking the direction, noise, vibration and current. All results are written on the job card.
markingPoints: Checks free turning and end float by hand
Winding continuity test with an ohmmeter
Insulation resistance test from windings to frame at a suitable voltage
Earth continuity from frame to the earth terminal or plug earth pin
Run test only after the dead tests pass, by a competent person on a protected bench; results recorded

essays.stem: Explain the main hazards when taking apart and reassembling electromechanical components, and how you would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: The biggest hazard is electric shock, so the equipment must be unplugged, or isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead, before work starts. Capacitors can hold a charge after the supply is off, so they are discharged with a resistor tool. Motors and gearboxes can be heavy, so two people or a lifting aid are used, with a straight back. Springs in contactors and relays are under tension and can fly out, so I wear safety glasses and hold the parts as I release them. Sharp edges on laminations, fan blades and covers can cut, so I wear gloves where it is safe to do so. Cleaning solvents can give off fumes and catch fire, so I use them in a ventilated area, away from flames, with gloves. Compressed air can blow dust into the eyes, so I use low pressure and eye protection. Parts may be hot after running, so I let them cool. Hammering can damage parts, so I use pullers and a soft-faced mallet.
markingPoints: Shock: unplug or isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead; discharge capacitors
Heavy parts: two people or a lifting aid
Springs and sharp edges: eye protection and gloves
Solvents and compressed air: ventilation, no flames, low pressure, eye protection
Hot parts and damage from hammering: let cool; use pullers and a soft-faced mallet

practical1.title: Dismantle, inspect and reassemble a small single-phase motor
practical1.brief: As a group, take apart, inspect and reassemble a small single-phase induction motor (or the motor of a pedestal fan) on the workshop bench. The motor is unplugged from any supply and its plug is kept in view on the bench. Before starting, the instructor shows how the capacitor (if fitted) is discharged with the Centre's resistor tool. Record the wiring with photos and labels, make match marks, and keep all parts in labelled trays. Remove the fan or pulley, the end shields and the rotor. Inspect the bearings, shaft, windings and centrifugal switch (if fitted) and write what you find on the job card. Reassemble in the reverse order, check that the shaft turns freely, then do the dead tests: winding continuity, insulation resistance from windings to frame, and earth continuity. The group does not connect the motor to a supply; any run test is done afterwards by the instructor on the protected test bench. Every member does at least one step of dismantling, one inspection check and one step of reassembly. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A small single-phase induction motor or pedestal fan motor, unplugged
Spanners, screwdrivers, hex keys, soft-faced mallet, gear puller, circlip pliers
Centre punch or marker for match marks; labels and parts trays
Soft brush and clean, lint-free cloths
Resistor discharge tool for capacitors (used as the instructor shows)
photos: The motor unplugged, with the plug in view, and the wiring labelled
Match marks on the end shields and frame
Parts laid out in labelled trays in order
The rotor removed, and the stator windings, showing what was inspected
The bearings and centrifugal switch (if fitted) being checked
The motor reassembled, with the shaft turned by hand
The dead test readings on the meter, and the completed job card
checklist: Kept the motor unplugged and took part in checking the capacitor was discharged
Recorded the wiring and made match marks before dismantling
Used the correct tools (puller, soft-faced mallet), with no hammering on the shaft or bearings
Removed the rotor without touching the windings
Inspected parts and wrote clear findings on the job card
Reassembled in reverse order, tightening bolts evenly in a criss-cross order
Checked the shaft turned freely and helped with the dead tests
Left the bench clean and returned all tools
safety: The motor stays unplugged for the whole task; it is never connected by the group
Capacitors are discharged with the resistor tool before anyone touches them
Wear safety glasses when using the puller and when releasing clips or springs
Lift heavy parts with two people; keep fingers clear of pinch points
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Dismantle, inspect and reassemble a contactor and a relay
practical2.brief: As a group, take apart, inspect and reassemble a contactor and a plug-in control relay on the bench. Neither is connected to any supply. Record the terminals and parts with photos, then remove the cover, contacts, armature and springs into labelled trays, taking care with the springs. Inspect the contacts for burning and pitting, the armature and magnet faces for dirt or damage, and the springs for breaks. Measure the coil resistance of each with an ohmmeter. If the instructor supplies a contact kit, fit it. Reassemble each item, check that the armature moves freely by hand, and use the ohmmeter to check that each contact opens and closes when the armature is pressed in by hand. Every member dismantles or reassembles at least one part, and each makes one meter check that another member records. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: One contactor and one plug-in relay with base (not connected to any supply)
Contact kit for the contactor, if available
Screwdrivers, long-nose pliers, parts trays and labels
Soft brush and clean, lint-free cloths
photos: The contactor and relay before dismantling, with terminal markings shown
Parts laid out in labelled trays
The contacts close up, showing their condition
The coil resistance reading on the meter
The contact kit being fitted (if used) and the items reassembled
A contact continuity check with the armature pressed in by hand
The completed job card, and the bench cleaned
checklist: Wore safety glasses and took care with springs under tension
Recorded the terminals and parts before dismantling
Kept the parts in order in labelled trays
Inspected contacts, armature, magnet faces and springs and recorded findings
Measured and recorded the coil resistance correctly
Reassembled so that the armature moves freely
Checked contacts open and close correctly with the ohmmeter
Left the bench clean and returned tools
safety: The contactor and relay are not connected to any supply during this task
Wear safety glasses; springs can fly out when released
Keep small parts in trays so none fall into drains or on the floor
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
